Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Jordan from Redwood Inference. We have Leah from our SE team with me. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Dr. Maya: Doing well, thanks. Excited to see what you have. We've been evaluating a couple options and wanted to understand the model catalog and how you recommend open models for our triage assistant use case.
[00:17] Jordan: Great. Quick agenda, we'll do a short product walkthrough of the Model Catalog, show some benchmark data, demonstrate the compatibility matrix and how to pick variants for latency vs cost, then Q&A and next steps. Is that ok?
[00:27] Alex: Yep, sounds good. We're especially interested in token cost and latency — we have 95th pct latency SLAs for the chat endpoint.
[00:33] Leah: Perfect. I'll share my screen — okay can everyone see the model catalog UI? I can scroll through curated models, filters for task (chat/generation/embeddings), and open model tags.
[00:43] [00:45] Leah: So here we have community and verified models; in the "open models" section we show recommended variants (fp16, int8) and pre-computed latency/cost estimates. Note these estimates are profiled on our runtime, actual numbers will vary by sequence length and batch size.
[00:58] Alex: When you say int8, is that post-training quantization? Any difference in hallucination rates you track?
[01:06] Leah: Good question. We have quantization-aware profiles — int8 here refers to 8-bit activation quantization using our runtime. We do regression checks using a set of eval prompts; the compatibility matrix flags models where quantization caused significant quality drops. It's not perfect but it's a good signal.
[01:21] Sam: For us, security is big — if we do a Dedicated or Private deployment, does the model catalog recommendations change? I mean, can we run the same quantized kernels on our VPC?
[01:30] Leah: Yes — the compatibility matrix includes columns for runtime capability, recommended kernel, and supported deployment modes. For Private/VPC we surface any dependencies (e.g., kernel libs) and whether we can bring the same optimized runtime. In most cases yes, but if you're on air-gapped on-prem there's a packaging step.
[01:44] Jordan: I'll call out an example: Mistral-ish open model X-1 (we sometimes call it X-one in notes) — it's very cost-effective at int8 and gives strong throughput. However, at long sequences and high retrieval contexts you might want fp16. Our console shows the switching tradeoff.
[01:58] Dr. Maya: Do you have benchmark numbers for our typical payloads? We do 512 token contexts most requests, occasionally 2k for summaries.
[02:07] Leah: We do. On the benchmark sheet I shared earlier, the 512-token steady state for variant X-1-int8 is around 45ms p50 and 220ms p95 on a T4-like node in our hosted environment; p95 is higher on 2k sequences. But we should run a pilot with your prompt set to get accurate numbers because content and prompting style matter.
[02:28] Alex: That 220ms p95 sounds good but our SLA is 150ms. Is Dedicated lower?
[02:33] Leah: Dedicated can lower variance because you get reserved capacity and reduced noisy neighbor effects — plus you can pick different GPU types. On A100-dense nodes we see p95 drop to ~130–160ms for similar setups. There's also room to tune batching and KV cache.
[02:48] [02:50] Jordan: Also remember caching: for conversational turn-taking we often keep a KV cache, and prefix caching can reduce per-token latency if you have repeated prompts. Our Optimize toolkit suggests caching configuration per route.
[03:03] Sam: On compliance, we need SOC 2 Type II, SSO/SAML, audit logs, and KMS integration. We also need to know retention — hosted logs retained 90 days? Can you redact PHI?
[03:14] Jordan: We support SOC 2, SSO/SAML, RBAC, and KMS keys via our Private offering or via dedicated key integrations for hosted with BYOK. Audit logs are available, retention is configurable as an add-on — typical hosted default is 90 days. Redaction: we recommend pre-processing to scrub PHI before sending to hosted endpoints; with Private you can keep everything in your VPC and do not send logs to Redwood. We'll send the security docs (SOC 2 report and data flows).
[03:38] Dr. Maya: Good. On model selection, how do you present compatibility matrix? Can you show an example?
[03:44] Leah: Sure. (scroll) The matrix rows are models/variants, columns include: task fit (chat/qa/embeddings), quantization impact, kernel availability, recommended deployment mode, p50/p95 latency estimates, tokens/sec throughput, and suggested prompt template. Cells sometimes show "warn" or "incompatible" if a kernel isn't supported on that hardware. You can export to CSV.
[04:07] Alex: Do you support ensemble/reranking flows? We do retrieval + generator + reranker sometimes.
[04:12] Leah: Yes — in the catalog you can compose routes: retrieval q->embed model, generator model, reranker model. We can pin different models for each step and set fallbacks. The runtime supports efficient batching across routes where possible.
[04:24] Jordan: Quick interjection — a common sales question: cost vs latency tradeoff. Typically int8 reduces cost per token 2–3x; fp16 preserves quality but costs more. For strict latency SLAs, Dedicated + A100 + tuned batching often wins.
[04:38] Dr. Maya: Any examples of customers in healthcare doing this?
[04:42] Jordan: Yes, a couple of clinics and an EMR partner — we had one customer run a pilot where they moved from hosted to Dedicated after seeing p95 improvements and better cost predictability for high throughput.
[04:54] [04:55] Alex: Let's talk benchmarks — you mentioned a spreadsheet earlier. Can you walk through how to read the benchmark rows?
[05:01] Leah: Absolutely. The spreadsheet has columns: model_variant, hardware, seq_len, batch_size, p50_latency_ms, p95_latency_ms, tokens_per_sec, memory_usage, noted regressions (if any), and eval_score on a set of quality prompts. Each row is a run; we annotate with runtime flags like kv_cache_enabled, continuous_batching, and quant_profile.
[05:21] Alex: What about cold-starts — does p95 include cold startup with cold KV?
[05:25] Leah: We separate cold vs steady-state in the benchmarks. The p95 we showed earlier was steady-state; cold starts are typically higher, and we recommend warmup strategies for latency-sensitive routes.
[05:35] Sam: On network and VPC, we have a strict egress policy — can Redwood run entirely within our VPC with no outgoing internet?
[05:42] Jordan: With Redwood Private you can run the control plane in your environment and the inference nodes can be air-gapped; there is a packaging step for the on-prem runtime. For hosted we do need egress but there are VPC peering options and private connections. We'll put details in the security pack.
[05:58] Dr. Maya: About hallucinations — you mentioned regression checks — do you provide evals and alerts if quality drops due to model changes or quantization?
[06:07] Leah: Yes, our Optimize product ties evals to routes. You can define test suites (prompt + expected behaviors), and we run continuous evals after model updates or rollout changes. Alerts trigger if eval scores drop below thresholds. We'll include an example eval set in the benchmark sheet.
[06:22] Alex: For our pilot, we want to run the same prompt set against three model variants and compare p95 and quality. Will the bench runner support that?
[06:30] Leah: Yes — our bench harness runs parallel tests across selected variants and exports comparative plots. We can run it in hosted for quick turn or in your Dedicated pool for representative numbers.
[06:40] Jordan: Let's cover pricing briefly — our hosted pay-as-you-go is per token plus model surcharge; Dedicated is reserved capacity with a monthly commit. We'll send a pricing deck with examples for your expected call volume.
[06:51] [06:53] Dr. Maya: Any hidden costs — e.g., storage for KV caches or extra logging charges?
[06:58] Jordan: Caching is included in the route cost, but long-term storage for logs/retention beyond default is an add-on. There's also a charge for high-retention audit logs and advanced observability. We'll mark those in the pricing deck.
[07:11] Alex: One practical question — our devs use Kubernetes and have certain GPU types; how battle-tested is your runtime on customers' on-prem clusters?
[07:19] Leah: We've deployed on customer on-prem k8s clusters and provided helm charts. The main differences are kernel-level optimizations and driver compat; we provide a compatibility checklist. If you're on older drivers we may recommend a node upgrade or using our Dedicated offering to avoid ops work.
[07:34] Sam: Ok. For the pilot we need a quick checklist — what do you need from us to run a representative benchmark?
[07:41] Leah: We'll need: sample prompt sets (PHI-scrubbed), target SLA numbers, typical sequence lengths, traffic profile (RPS), and network constraints (VPC/firewall). Also access for a benchmark runner — we can do it with a secure token.
[07:56] Dr. Maya: We'll provide that. One more thing: are there any licensing or export restrictions on some open models we should be aware of?
[08:02] Jordan: Yes some models have license clauses — the catalog flags license types (permissive/mitigation required). We'll include license notes in the compatibility export.
[08:12] Alex: Can we get an example of the compatibility CSV?
[08:15] Leah: I'll attach it after the call — it includes model, variant, recommended kernel, quantization support, recommended node type, p50/p95, and flags for private-deploy readiness.
[08:25] [08:27] Jordan: Quick demo note — when you click a model entry there's a "profiling" link that shows detailed traces and the benchmark runs that produced those numbers. You can filter by sequence length and hardware.
[08:39] Dr. Maya: If we start with hosted to move fast, then move to Dedicated later, how disruptive is that?
[08:46] Leah: We've built the abstraction so you can pin the same model version and rollout policy across environments. In practice moving from hosted to Dedicated is mostly operational (provisioning nodes) and requires a config change — not code changes. There are a few caveats for on-prem kernels but we'll outline them.
[09:00] Alex: About fallbacks — can you set automatic fallback to a cheaper model when Dedicated capacity is saturated?
[09:06] Jordan: Yes, our smart routing can policy-route to fallback models by latency/cost/region. You can set a policy like prefer Dedicated A100, fallback to hosted cheaper variant, with automated throttles.
[09:18] Sam: Good. Any concerns about model drift monitoring if we use open models?
[09:22] Leah: Drift monitoring is supported via the Optimize tooling — we track quality metrics and prompt-histograms; you can set alerts per-route. For open models we'd recommend scheduled re-evals when you change quantization or kernel.
[09:34] [09:36] Jordan: We're about half hour in — do you want to dive into any part deeper?
[09:40] Alex: I'd like to see the benchmark sheet now if possible.
[09:43] Leah: (shares) Here's the sheet. You'll see three example models X-1, Y-2, Z-3, with int8 and fp16 rows. Note the compatibility flags — Z-3-int8 shows a slight quality regression on our medical QA set.
[09:56] Dr. Maya: Can you quantify "slight"?
[09:58] Leah: On our eval suite, Z-3-int8 drops accuracy from 88% to 82% on certain question types. We flag that — for patient-facing summaries we generally avoid that variant.
[10:12] Alex: Ok. For the triage assistant, accuracy on dosing/exam interpretation is critical, so maybe X-1-fp16 or Y-2-int8 with manual post-filtering?
[10:21] Leah: Exactly. Many teams pick a higher-quality variant for the generator and use a smaller, cheaper model for reranking or retrieval where strict accuracy isn't as critical.
[10:30] Sam: Do you support function/tool-calling patterns? We have structured outputs to feed back into our workflow engine.
[10:36] Leah: Yes — the API supports structured outputs and function/tool-calls, JSON schema enforcement and response validation. That integrates with the console routes.
[10:44] Jordan: Alright, wrapping up — agreed next steps are in the action items: Jordan will send pricing and hosting vs dedicated comparison, Leah will share the compatibility matrix and attach the benchmark CSV, NewHope team will send sample prompts and network constraints and we'll schedule a pilot kickoff.
[10:58] Dr. Maya: Sounds good. Any final questions?
[11:02] Alex: None from me. Thanks for the thorough demo.
[11:05] Sam: Thanks. We'll target the due dates and get the prompts over.
[11:09] Jordan: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up via email with the docs and calendar invite for the pilot.
[11:14] Leah: Thanks all. Bye.
